lessons.title: Lesson 1: What machine learning is
lessons.text:
Lesson 1 of 6 · about 4 minutes
Goal: Explain machine learning in your own words and spot it in daily life.
This lesson builds toward: Without notes, you will explain what machine learning is and identify whether a task is classification or regression, with a correct explanation and at least 4 of 5 tasks sorted correctly.
In normal programming a person writes the rules. In machine learning (ML), you give the computer many examples with the right answers, and it finds the rules itself. The result is called a model.
Everyday examples: your email learns what spam looks like from millions of marked emails. A music app suggests songs from what people like you played. A map app predicts traffic from past trips.
Two common jobs: classification puts things in groups (spam or not spam, which kind of flower). Regression predicts a number (house price, minutes until the bus comes). When the examples come with answers, it is called supervised learning, and that is what this course teaches.
Words to know:
- Machine learning (ML): computers finding patterns in examples instead of following rules a person wrote.
- Model: what ML produces: a set of learned patterns that makes predictions.
- Classification: predicting a group or category.
- Regression: predicting a number.
- Supervised learning: learning from examples that come with the right answers.
Try it now: List three apps you use that probably use machine learning. For each one, write what it predicts and whether that is classification (a group) or regression (a number).
You can now explain what machine learning is and tell classification from regression.

check.q: In machine learning, what is a model?
options: A list of rules a person typed by hand
The result of a computer finding patterns in examples
check.why: The model is what the computer produces after finding patterns in examples.

check.q: A shop wants to sort customer emails into "complaint" or "question". Which kind of job would you call this?
check.why: Putting things into groups is classification; predicting a number is regression.

lessons.title: Lesson 2: Data: features and labels
lessons.text:
Lesson 2 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Build a small dataset with features and a label.
This lesson builds toward: Given a prediction problem, you will create a small dataset with sensible features and a label and check it for gaps, with features that affect the answer, one label column and at least one possible gap named.
ML learns from data, usually a table. Each row is one example. The columns that describe the example are features. The column with the answer you want to predict is the label.
Example: to predict if a bus will be late, each row is one trip. Features might be time of day, day of the week and whether it rained. The label is late or on time.
Good features are things that really affect the answer. More rows usually help. The data must also be fair and complete: if you only collect weekday trips, the model will be bad at weekends. A model can only be as good as its data.
Step by step:
- Decide what you want to predict: that is your label.
- List things that might affect it: those are your features.
- Make a table with one row per example.
- Fill in at least 10 rows from real life.
- Check: are some kinds of examples missing?
Words to know:
- Dataset: a collection of examples, usually a table.
- Feature: a column that describes an example, used to make the prediction.
- Label: the answer column the model learns to predict.
- Bias in data: when the data leaves out or over-counts some groups, so the model is unfair or wrong for them.
Try it now: Pick something you can predict from daily life, such as whether you will be tired after practice or whether a store will be busy. Make a table with two or three features and a label, and fill in 10 rows.
You can now pick a label and useful features and build a small dataset.

check.q: In a data table, what are features?
options: The columns that describe each example
The answer you want to predict
check.why: Features describe the example; the label is the answer to predict.

check.q: You collect data on which students finish homework, but only from one class. What would you do before training?
options: Train right away; one class is enough for everyone
Collect data from more classes so the model is fair to other students
Only use the first five rows
check.why: Data from one group can make the model poor or unfair for others.

lessons.title: Lesson 3: Training and testing: is the model any good?
lessons.text:
Lesson 3 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Split data into a training set and a test set and measure accuracy.
This lesson builds toward: Given a dataset and a model's test results, you will explain why data is split into training and test sets and calculate accuracy, with the accuracy correct to the nearest whole percent.
Training is when the model studies examples to find patterns. But a model that only memorized its examples could look perfect and still fail on new ones. That is called overfitting, like a student who memorized last year's test answers.
So you hold some data back. The training set (often about 75 to 80 percent of the rows) is used to learn. The test set (the rest) is hidden until the end and used to check the model on examples it has never seen.
Accuracy is the share of test examples it got right. 18 right out of 20 is 90 percent. Always ask what a mistake costs: a wrong song suggestion is fine, a missed fraud alert is not.
Step by step:
- Shuffle your rows.
- Put about 75 percent in the training set.
- Keep the rest as the test set and do not look at it.
- Find a pattern (a rule) from the training set only.
- Use it on the test set and count how many it got right.
Words to know:
- Training: the model learning patterns from examples.
- Training set: the rows used for learning.
- Test set: rows held back to check the model on new examples.
- Overfitting: when a model memorizes its training data and does badly on new data.
- Accuracy: the share of predictions that were right.
Try it now: Take your 10-row table from Lesson 2. Cover the last 2 rows. From the first 8, write one simple rule (for example "if it rained, the bus is late"). Test the rule on the 2 hidden rows and work out the accuracy.
You can now split data into training and test sets and calculate accuracy.

options: When a model is too small
When there is too much test data
When a model memorizes its training examples and fails on new ones
check.why: Overfitting is like memorizing last year's test answers.

check.q: A fraud model gets 95% accuracy, but the misses are real fraud. What would you ask next?
options: Can we skip the test set?
Can we train on the test set?
check.why: Always ask what a mistake costs; a missed fraud alert matters a lot.

chapters.name: Chapter 2: Training your first model in Colab

lessons.title: Lesson 4: Loading a dataset with scikit-learn
lessons.text:
Lesson 4 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Load a practice dataset in Colab and look at its features and labels.
This lesson builds toward: In Google Colab with scikit-learn, you will load a practice dataset and describe its rows, features and labels, naming the number of rows and columns and what the label means.
scikit-learn is a free Python library for machine learning, already installed in Google Colab. It comes with small practice datasets. The iris dataset has 150 flowers. Each has four features (length and width of two parts of the flower, in centimeters) and a label: one of three species.
Load it with: from sklearn.datasets import load_iris, then iris = load_iris(). The features are in iris.data and the labels in iris.target. iris.feature_names and iris.target_names tell you what the columns and labels mean.
Always look at your data before training: how many rows, what the columns are, and a few example rows. iris.data.shape tells you rows and columns: (150, 4).
Step by step:
- Open a new notebook at colab.research.google.com.
- Run: from sklearn.datasets import load_iris
- Run: iris = load_iris()
- Print iris.data.shape, iris.feature_names and iris.target_names.
- Print the first three rows: print(iris.data[:3], iris.target[:3])
Words to know:
- scikit-learn: a free Python library for machine learning, imported as sklearn.
- Iris dataset: a famous practice dataset of 150 flowers in three species.
- shape: the number of rows and columns in the data.
- X and y: common names: X for the features, y for the labels.
Official sources:
- scikit-learn: Getting Started
- Google Colab: Frequently Asked Questions
Try it now: Load the iris dataset in Colab. Print the shape, the four feature names, the three species names, and the first five rows with their labels. Write down which number stands for which species.
You can now load a dataset in Colab and describe its features, labels and size.

check.q: In scikit-learn's iris dataset, what does iris.target hold?
check.why: iris.target holds the labels; iris.data holds the features.

check.q: You just loaded a new dataset. What would you do before training a model?
options: Look at the shape, the column names and a few example rows
check.why: Always look at your data before training.

lessons.title: Lesson 5: Training and testing a decision tree
lessons.text:
Lesson 5 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Split the data, train a decision tree, and measure its accuracy.
This lesson builds toward: Given the iris dataset, you will split the data, train a decision tree and print its accuracy on the test set, with the code running without errors and the accuracy printed.
A decision tree learns a set of yes-or-no questions, like a flowchart: "Is the petal shorter than 2.5 cm? Then it is species 0." It is easy to explain, which makes it a good first model.
Every scikit-learn model works the same way: create it, fit it on training data, then predict on new data. The code: X, y = load_iris(return_X_y=True). X_train, X_test, y_train, y_test = train_test_split(X, y, test_size=0.25, random_state=42). model = DecisionTreeClassifier(random_state=42). model.fit(X_train, y_train).
Then test it: predictions = model.predict(X_test) and print(accuracy_score(y_test, predictions)). random_state=42 just fixes the shuffle so you get the same result every time you run it.
Step by step:
- Import: from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split
- Import: from sklearn.tree import DecisionTreeClassifier
- Import: from sklearn.metrics import accuracy_score
- Split with train_test_split(X, y, test_size=0.25, random_state=42).
- Create the model, call model.fit(X_train, y_train), then predict on X_test and print the accuracy.
Words to know:
- Decision tree: a model that learns a flowchart of yes-or-no questions.
- fit: train the model on data.
- predict: use the trained model to guess labels for new data.
- train_test_split: the scikit-learn tool that splits data into training and test sets.
- random_state: a number that fixes the random shuffle so results repeat.
Official sources:
- scikit-learn: Getting Started
Try it now: Type and run the full decision tree code in Colab. Print the accuracy. Then change test_size to 0.5, run it again, and write down whether accuracy went up or down.
You can now split data, train a decision tree with fit, predict with it and measure accuracy.

check.q: Why is a decision tree a good first model?
options: It is easy to explain, like a flowchart of yes-or-no questions
check.why: A decision tree's questions can be read like a flowchart.

check.q: You trained your model and want to check it. Which line would you run?
check.why: Predict on the test set, then compare with the true labels for accuracy.

lessons.title: Lesson 6: Comparing models and knowing their limits
lessons.text:
Lesson 6 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Train a second model, compare it with the first, predict a new example and name a limit.
This lesson builds toward: Given two trained models, you will compare their test accuracy, predict a new example and write one limit of your chosen model, choosing a model with a reason and naming a real limit.
There is rarely one perfect model, so you try more than one. k-nearest neighbors (KNN) predicts by finding the k most similar examples in the training data and taking a vote. Create it with KNeighborsClassifier(n_neighbors=5) from sklearn.neighbors; it uses the same fit and predict steps.
Compare both models on the same test set. To predict one new flower, give the model a list inside a list: model.predict([[5.1, 3.5, 1.4, 0.2]]). It returns the species number; iris.target_names turns it into a name.
Know the limits. These models only know these three species and these four measurements: show them a rose and they will still name an iris. A small test set can make accuracy look better or worse than it is. And with real data about people, check that the model works fairly for every group before anyone relies on it.
Step by step:
- Import: from sklearn.neighbors import KNeighborsClassifier
- Create knn = KNeighborsClassifier(n_neighbors=5) and fit it on the same training data.
- Print both accuracy scores.
- Predict one new flower with the better model: model.predict([[5.1, 3.5, 1.4, 0.2]])
- Write which model you would choose and one limit.
Words to know:
- k-nearest neighbors (KNN): a model that predicts by a vote of the most similar training examples.
- n_neighbors: how many similar examples KNN looks at (the k).
- Limit: a case the model cannot handle well.
- Fairness: a model working equally well for every group of people it affects.
Official sources:
- scikit-learn: Getting Started
Try it now: Final task: in one notebook, train the decision tree and a KNN model on the same split, print both accuracies, predict the species of the flower [6.0, 2.9, 4.5, 1.5] with the better model and print its name, then write two sentences on which model you chose and one limit it has.
You can now train, test and compare two models, make a prediction, and explain a model's limits.
How your final task is checked:
What we look at Not yet Meets Exceeds Loading and splitting the data The data does not load, or the model is tested on the training data. The iris data is loaded and split into training and test sets with train_test_split. Also prints the shape of each set and explains the split. Two models trained and tested Only one model is trained, or accuracy is missing. A decision tree and a KNN model are trained, and each one's test accuracy is printed. Also tries a second value of n_neighbors and compares. Prediction for a new flower No prediction, or the input is in the wrong shape. The better model predicts one new flower and the species name is printed. Also explains why the prediction makes sense from the measurements. Choice and limits The two sentences are missing, or no real limit is named. Two sentences: which model and why, and one real limit. Also mentions the cost of mistakes or fairness for data about people. To pass: Meets or Exceeds on every row. If a row is Not yet, fix that part and try again.

check.q: What does n_neighbors=5 mean in a KNN model?
options: It looks at the 5 most similar training examples and takes a vote
check.why: KNN predicts by a vote of the k most similar examples.

check.q: Your model predicted species 0 for a new flower. How would you turn that number into a name?
check.why: iris.target_names turns the species number into a name.
